title: Sadie Sink and Maya Hawke Star in Hand-Drawn Prada Campaign by Legendary Disney Animator John Pomeroy

	At a time
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	At a time when AI has become more pervasive in advertising, a return to traditional techniques can feel like an act of rebellion. Those methods may come with steeper production costs but are proving worthwhile for brands like Prada, whose new hand-drawn holiday campaign has drawn widespread praise online since debut Wednesday night.

	For its 2026 holiday campaign, aptly titled “Drawing Prada: Animated by Hand,” the Italian fashion house enlisted veteran Disney animator John Pomeroy to create a hand-drawn winter wonderland starring Sadie Sink, Maya Hawke, Kelvin Harrison Jr., Chen Haoyu and Luther Ford.




	The campaign, conceived under creative directors Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons, combines live-action photography with traditional pencil-and-paper animation, placing its cast alongside illustrated woodland creatures in a series of whimsical holiday scenes. In one image, Sink encounters a group of mice attempting to carry off a polka-dot Prada loafer, while another features Hawke alongside an animated fox in a snowy forest.

	Pomeroy, whose decades-long animation career includes work on Disney’s “Pocahontas,” “Fantasia 2000” and “The Land Before Time,” led a team of artists using traditional hand-drawing techniques to create the campaign’s animated characters and landscapes. Photographer Glen Luchford shot the actors with lighting and perspectives designed to match the illustrated environments.

	“There’s a very distinct and purposeful reason to do hand-drawn animation, and that’s to see that there’s value in the human touch,” Pomeroy said in a behind-the-scenes video released by Prada. “And that hand-drawn and handcrafted work is still alive in the world today.”


	The campaign arrives as the fashion and advertising industries continue to experiment with generative AI, raising questions about the future of traditional creative work. According to a 2026 report from the Interactive Advertising Bureau, nearly two-thirds of digital video ad buyers now use generative AI in creative production, up from roughly half in 2025. Coca-Cola, meanwhile, has faced backlash for its AI-generated holiday commercials, which it produced for two consecutive years in 2024 and 2025.

	The project also marks a continuation of Prada’s longstanding relationship with cinema. Last year’s holiday campaign, “A Winter’s Tale,” similarly featured Hawke in a cinematic winter setting photographed by Luchford, though this year’s installment trades its more conventional live-action imagery for an illustrated fantasy.

	The campaign’s still images, short films and behind-the-scenes footage are available on Prada’s website.

title: Aliens, Dinosaurs and a Father’s Death: ‘Kefi’ Director Saito Kisin Brings a Surreal Take on Grief to Tokyo
description: Likely the strangest entry at this year’s Tokyo International Film Festival, the surreal “Kefi,” the debut feature by cinematographer Saito Kisin,
body:
Likely the strangest entry at this year’s Tokyo International Film Festival, the surreal “Kefi,” the debut feature by cinematographer Saito Kisin, mixes multiple short stories and multiple styles to make sense of the feelings around a complicated relationship with his late father. 

	It doesn’t get there through the signifiers one might anticipate: there are aliens, dinosaurs, dream affairs and more across the film’s compact runtime. “Kefi” plays in the festival’s Nippon Cinema Now section.
	

	“Initially, I wanted to do four series of short films and put it together, and that would become a feature,” Saito says. “And those four would all have individual themes. So the first one would be ethics. Second would be hypocrisy. There would be discrimination, and fourth would be life and death.”

	The youngest of three brothers, Saito intended to loosely connect the project to his own family, with his shorts following three sisters instead. Then, in 2024, he received news that his father had died.

	That news is echoed in the film’s opening. Shortly after a scene in which their absent father speaks about them in narration, an echo from beyond the grave, three sisters – oldest Kyo, middle child Asumi and youngest Kino – learn of his death. Like Saito’s own father, the girls’ father had been separated from the family since their parents’ divorce.

	“To tell you the truth, when my father passed, I didn’t feel sad,” Saito says. “Well, the reason being my parents divorced about 10 years ago, I haven’t met him for about 10 or so years.”
	

	The film’s listing in the Tokyo program is upfront about its aim to explore the complicated feelings that follow a loss, including numbness. Saito explores that through the oddball humor that drives much of “Kefi.”

	“I’m an optimistic person; my father was a very funny guy. That also added to the fact that there wasn’t much grief in his loss, and I thought that I would meet again with him and talk with him again soon, but that became so sudden,” Saito says. “I realized that not everybody goes through grief when they lose their loved ones. So that idea came to me, and I wanted to depict that perspective through the three sisters.”

	The three sisters spend much of the film’s runtime apart, rather than the film exploring an overlapping dynamic between them. “Just because you’re family, you’re not always together, it’s not like you always share something, always,” Saito says. “Your siblings lead their separate lives, but at the very end, siblings or families think about the same things or have the same mindset.” One episode of the film eventually reunites them.

	Those differences are embodied in the mixed visual approaches Saito takes, switching between vivid color and monochrome, and between chaotic handheld work and steadier camerawork. He didn’t set out to assign those looks along thematic lines, though he says the result allowed the imagery to carry different nuances. “It’s only because I wanted to test and try different approaches. That’s why it ended up as it is,” he says, adding: “I think it’s important that people stay interested and will be attentive.”

	Saito’s experiments come from his hands-on approach – he is credited as director, writer, cinematographer, gaffer and editor – and taking on those roles mostly comes down to comfort, as it’s the way he knows how to make films. “That’s why my style is to use a single-lens reflex camera, I use iMovie and have my friends appear as actors. That’s what I use for YouTube, and I work behind the camera on bigger productions as well,” he says. “But when you’re on a big set with bigger productions, sometimes not everybody’s looking in the same direction, and so sometimes that becomes kind of a noise when you’re trying to make a film. And so what I really wanted to do was make a film only with people I really trust.”
	

	The making of “Kefi” also perhaps reflects a desire to show a range of approaches that stand out from the international understanding of Japanese film.

	“When you think about Japanese films done by Japanese people, people would imagine anime or films with [mainstream appeal],” Saito says. “But I think that’s a shame. I feel that there’s more interesting, more funny, more unique Japanese people in the world, so I really want to show that to people around the world through film.”

	Saito says his multiple roles on the film may convey his point of view more directly to the audience. “I just want to prove that Japanese films are not only about those classic filmmakers like Ozu or Kurosawa, but there are more modern people like Hamaguchi, or even myself. That is my aspiration.”

title: ‘Godzilla Minus One’ U.S. Success ‘Wasn’t a Strategy; We Just Tried,’ Says Toho CEO at Tokyo Festival
description: Japanese studio giant Toho’s North American release of “Godzilla Minus One” was a turning point in the company’s approach to the global market, CEO
body:
Japanese studio giant Toho’s North American release of “Godzilla Minus One” was a turning point in the company’s approach to the global market, CEO Matsuoka Hiro said at the Tokyo International Film Festival on Thursday.

	Matsuoka was speaking at an “Academy in Tokyo” session with Bill Kramer, CEO of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. The film went on to gross $57.1 million in North America.


	The result grew out of an opportunity Matsuoka encountered during a U.S. trip. In conversations with exhibitors, he heard that Hollywood studios were not making enough films to meet audience demand. They suggested Toho consider anime; Matsuoka said the discussions helped him recognize the popularity of Japanese animation in the U.S. Since Toho already had “Godzilla,” the company decided to take the franchise to the market itself.
	

	The move was not an obvious one inside Toho. Matsuoka said colleagues were concerned when he proposed the U.S. release, as the company had previously struggled to distribute its films successfully outside Japan. But the film performed well, and, he said, the revenue returned to Toho.

	“It was all a coincidence,” Matsuoka said of the opportunity. “It wasn’t a strategy; we just tried.”

	For Matsuoka, the experience showed the value of testing new approaches as Toho expands its international business. Toho’s follow-up, Yamazaki Takashi’s “Godzilla Minus Zero,” will open in Japan on Nov. 3 and in North America on Nov. 6 through Gkids, the U.S. distributor Toho acquired in 2024.

	The broader conversation turned to how theatrical exhibition and streaming can serve different roles in reaching audiences. Matsuoka said the two are “more like coexisting than enemies.” He noted that Japanese cinemas have drawn audiences back since the pandemic with repertory screenings, including retrospectives of Miyazaki Hayao’s films.
	

	Kramer pointed to “Parasite” as evidence of a more global film culture, recalling director Bong Joon Ho’s remarks about audiences becoming more open to subtitles and films in other languages. Kramer also said theatrical exhibition can introduce younger generations to film history, while streaming gives films another life after their cinema run.

	Asked about Asia’s share of the global film market, Kramer called the region “an extremely important market” and said it was a key reason for the Academy’s presence in Tokyo. He said 25% of the Academy’s voting members are based outside the U.S. and described partnerships with film festivals as a way to bring members together and reach potential members. The Academy’s work, he added, extends beyond the Oscars to educating people and inviting them to engage with the film industry.

	The executives also addressed artificial intelligence. Matsuoka called AI a tool that could maximize workflow, while cautioning that companies should keep a close eye on its effects. Kramer said that, as the industry evolves, the Academy continues to reward human authorship and creation.

schema.headline: ‘Godzilla Minus One’ U.S. Success ‘Wasn’t a Strategy; We Just Tried,’ Says Toho CEO at Tokyo Festival

title: ‘Ninja Warrior’ Maker TBS Tells Tokyo Market How Legendary, CJ ENM Alliances Fit Its Push to Make J-Content the Next K-Drama
description: A Thursday morning session at TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival, highlighted the Tokyo Broadcasting System (TBS)
body:
A Thursday morning session at TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival, highlighted the Tokyo Broadcasting System (TBS) Group’s initiatives to find global footholds for Japanese content and “inspiring global love for Japan.” 

	Watanabe Shinya, president of the global business division at TBS Holdings, and Setoguchi Katsuaki, executive officer of the global business division at TBS Holdings and president and CEO of The Seven and The Seven U.S., spoke about how the group is working to accelerate its global business.
	

	The session began by highlighting TBS Group’s global partnerships, particularly with Legendary Entertainment, and with South Korea’s CJ ENM and Japanese streamer U-Next on new joint venture Studio Monowa. Setoguchi spoke about his ongoing interest in Korean programming and content, recalling that 20 years ago he saw a gap between the production capabilities of Korean and Japanese studios, and that, “to my embarrassment,” he had not anticipated the now vast influence of Korean cultural output. “Everywhere you go around the world, K-content and K-drama, they are a part of everybody’s everyday lives,” he said.

	Setoguchi said he sees his mission as spreading Japanese content worldwide to a similar extent, and that “instead of working to generate a profit to TBS, I would be working to establish a new genre of J-content.” After calling on the Japanese industry to work together to find global reach for Japanese IP, he spoke about how TBS is connecting with the North American market, noting its $150 million equity investment in Legendary Entertainment earlier this year.
	

	TBS Group partnered with Legendary because of what Setoguchi described as “matching needs” – TBS wants to create global hits in global markets, while Legendary is “keeping a close eye on the potential of Japanese IP,” including manga, anime and novels, with a view to adapting them into live action. In the partnership, TBS is to “play the role of cultural translator” for Legendary.

	Looking to cultivate markets beyond the West, the discussion then moved to TBS’s partners in Asia. Studio Monowa, its joint venture with CJ ENM and U-Next Holdings, sees TBS Group “combined with CJ ENM’s global standard production capabilities” to develop IP that resonates with the world.

	Variety content and game shows are also a key focus of the group’s efforts to build a foothold for Japanese content in other countries, with Banijay Entertainment partnering on local adaptations of “Sasuke: Ninja Warrior.”

	“Ninja Warrior” is providing something of a template for new IP such as “Kasso,” a skateboarding-focused spin on the same sports entertainment game show formula.

	“‘Kasso’ was not created in the mere framework of a TV program. From the beginning, it has been planned as a street culture IP,” Setoguchi said, pointing to rollouts in the U.S. and China.

	Setoguchi also described his ambitions for The Seven, aiming for it to be a studio that “creates the next obsession that the world will go wild for,” with its production collaboration on “Alice in Borderland” as a starting point. “The challenge we are taking on goes on into 2030, and beyond into 2040,” he said. Beyond the American, European and Asian markets, he added, the company has ambitions toward uncultivated markets in Africa.

	Watanabe then took over, laying out the worldwide reach of “Sasuke: Ninja Warrior,” now in its third decade on air, with local adaptations in 25 countries. They include NBC’s “American Ninja Warrior,” which is in its 18th season, with Seasons 19 and 20 already greenlit.

	“It’s the very first TBS sports entertainment which has aired globally,” Watanabe said. “It continues to grow globally.” The show now reaches 170 countries.

	Clips from global partners drove the point home. James Townley, chief content officer, development, at Banijay Entertainment, spoke about the brand value of “Ninja Warrior” and its “clear format USP.” Ella Brahmachari, ITV Studios’ brand manager for “Ninja Warrior UK” said the show is aspirational, and that because the athletes are amateurs rather than professionals, audiences feel involved. Thomas Goseberg of RTL Studios, which produces the German adaptation, said a second golden age of the show is coming, and that its appeal lies in the sense of challenge and accomplishment.
	

	Watanabe flagged upcoming anniversaries for the show, including its 30th in 2027. He also pointed to the show inspiring a new obstacle discipline in modern pentathlon at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

	He then talked about pursuing a “360-degree experience” for the brand through indoor parks in the U.K., Germany and the U.S., merchandise and licensing, and placement advertising within the show and its local adaptations.

	Exporting these properties as IP with room to expand was the priority, Watanabe said. Toward the end of his presentation, he pointed to TBS’s overseas bases, The Seven in Los Angeles and TBS International in New York, and to plans for bases in Europe to strengthen sales.

	Anime came up as an example of the global reach of Japanese culture, which TBS hopes to recreate with other formats. “Anime and manga are globally very popular,” Setoguchi said earlier in the session, though he does not think that “J-content is also accepted on the same level.”

	To get there, the TBS executives said, they need to “create a market from scratch, and then grow the market” for a “new category of J-content.”

title: Animated Movie Based on Bestseller ‘The Unicorn That Said No’ Travels to Multiple Territories Ahead of AFM (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Sales agency The Playmaker Munich has closed distribution deals for the animated movie “The Unicorn That Said No” in several territories, ahead of
body:
Sales agency The Playmaker Munich has closed distribution deals for the animated movie “The Unicorn That Said No” in several territories, ahead of its market premiere at the American Film Market in Los Angeles.

	The feature has been sold to Unlimited Media for the Baltic states, WWE Rights for Benelux, KMBO for France, Grand Entertainment for Motion Pictures for the Middle East, M2 Films for Poland, Idea Film for Romania, Another World Entertainment for Scandinavia, Pack Magic for Spain and Orjinlab for Turkey.
	

	The German distributor is Warner Bros. Film Productions Germany, with a release on Jan. 1, 2027.

	“The Unicorn That Said No” is based on the book “Das Neinhorn” by Marc-Uwe Kling and Astrid Henn, which has been translated into more than 25 languages.

	The movie centers on a “sweet, grumpy unicorn” who can no longer bear the pink, idyllic world of his unicorn family and sets off for Nowhere. He unexpectedly finds new friends and together they must rescue the king’s daughter from her tower in order to return home with his new gang.

	The movie is directed by Kling, Johannes Weiland (“The Gruffalo’s Child”) and Studio Soi, with a screenplay by Kling and Marcus Sauermann.

	Kling also lends his voice to the unicorn. The German voice cast also features Nora Tschirner, Torsten Sträter and Karoline Herfurth.

	The movie is a production of X Filme Creative Pool (“Run Lola Run,” “Goodbye, Lenin!”) and Studio Soi (“The Gruffalo,” “The Wonderfully Weird World of Gumball”), in co-production with Warner Bros. Film Productions Germany. Producers are Uwe Schott, Nicole Kellerhals and Carsten Bunte. Co-producers are Steffen Schier, Margret Mackuth and Julia Hayungs. Music is by Felix Raffel, and the main song is by Dota Kehr.
	

	The movie is supported by MFG, MDM, BKM, FFA and Kuratorium Junger Deutscher Film.

	The market premiere will be at 11 a.m. on Nov. 11 at AMC Century City in Los Angeles. The Playmaker Munich will be based at the Fairmont Century Plaza, Los Angeles during AFM.

	Sylvia Edelmann, head of sales at The Playmaker, said, “It’s wonderful to see so many territories on board before the film has even screened. The book is a hit with readers of all ages around the world, and we can’t wait to bring this sweet, grumpy unicorn to even more audiences at AFM.”

schema.headline: Animated Movie Based on Bestseller ‘The Unicorn That Said No’ Travels to Multiple Territories Ahead of AFM (EXCLUSIVE)

title: AI Can Critique Shakespeare but Can’t Write It, Russo Brothers’ AGBO Execs Tell Tokyo Market
description: Top AGBO execs Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes delivered a keynote discussion at TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo International Film Fest
body:
Top AGBO execs Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes delivered a keynote discussion at TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival, on Thursday, about how AI is impacting filmmaking, how it can be used to assist rather than replace human creators and how it will shape the future of visual content creation.

	Brearton is a partner and business leader at AGBO, while Hughes is the company’s chief scientific officer and technology leader.
	

	Headquartered in Los Angeles, AGBO focuses on producing cross-platform entertainment properties, including such films as “Extraction” (2020), “Everything Everywhere All at Once” (2022), “The Gray Man” (2022), “Extraction 2” (2023) and “The Electric State” (2025).

	Brearton noted that early in their careers, AGBO founders Anthony and Joe Russo were working on the Emmy-winning comedy hit “Arrested Development” when they received a script for the show that would ordinarily be too long and expensive to produce. Instead of giving it a pass, they used digital cameras and editing to make it a reality. “They looked at technology as a solution that empowered them to tell the story they wanted to tell,” said Brearton. And that way of thinking is now in the corporate DNA of AGBO.

	Another inspiration for AGBO’s business philosophy, Brearton added, was Walt Disney, who brought Disney characters to life in another medium – the theme park – for the enjoyment of fans. “In 2026 we are using technology to build a virtual theme park, a virtual community bringing people together,” he said.
	

	AGBO also recognizes that “creative artists are special,” Brearton added: “Humans are uniquely positioned to tell stories. The way we embrace technology is all about artists and putting artists first.”

	Hughes used the example of Pixar, which evolved technology around 3D rendering. “But technology was not sufficient on its own,” he said. “They used it to tell incredible stories. Technology played a supporting role. That’s how we think about these things at AGBO.”

	Hughes, who has a strong academic background in algorithms and machine learning, described being an ardent fan of Disney cartoons as a child and spending his teenage years “going down the rabbit hole” of 3D rendering and video game creation. He also had a musical talent, playing cello for orchestras.

	This creative side, Hughes said, has found an outlet in his career at what he calls “the intersection of media and technology.” His background informs his belief that, in creative fields, “you have to have a human that’s sitting on top and curating to make sure the algorithms are not running on their own.” At AGBO, he said, his role “is really about supporting artists to be more and more creative.”

	Brearton added that AGBO wants to make sure the artists and creatives feel comfortable. “At our LA studio you’ll see our technologists and our creatives really sitting side by side, working together,” he said.

	But excitement about what AI can do in supporting content creation is accompanied by anxiety about an AI-dominated future. Brearton responded that “there is a lot of misinformation” about AI’s role.

	“There’s a concern that it’s going to replace us all,” he said. But what makes a favorite performance by a favorite actor special, he added, “is the human element” that AI cannot equal. “AI is really going to be more impactful, particularly in the midterm, in process efficiencies,” he said.

	That is, using AI to fix problems and do work that slows and impedes the creative process. “We really think it’s an empowerment,” said Brearton. Instead of replacing artists, Hughes added, AI is “making them better storytellers.” With AI, he explained, “you can handle all the annoying things that keep you from enjoying yourself [as a creator].”
	

	Also, the arrival of artificial general intelligence (AGI) does not mean the doom of creative artists, Hughes said. Instead, “people who are at the pinnacle of their arts” – the Brahmses and Beethovens – cannot be replicated by a machine, no matter how smart. At AGBO, he said, “the technologists are helping creatives build tools” that enhance their creativity and increase their productivity, not take their jobs.

	AI, Hughes noted, is good at “regurgitating what has been done in the past,” but not good at creating something from scratch. “Machines don’t have the creativity required for that degree of novelty,” he said.

	AI, however, “is good at critiquing,” Hughes observed. AI can tell you whether a play someone discovered in an attic might have been written by Shakespeare, but if you ask it to write its own Shakespeare play, “you’d have the sense that it was written by a 12-year-old,” he said.

	Another example of how AI can support the creative process is scriptwriting. “If you’re struggling a little bit with a character in the third act, it can provide data,” Brearton said. “Not a solution, but data.”

	AI can also help “democratize storytelling,” Brearton noted: “We’ll see new filmmakers making movies that otherwise you wouldn’t have seen” because AI has helped them achieve their vision on a budget they can afford.

	At the same time, Hughes added, AI can generate endless amounts of mediocre content, “but consumers can’t possibly absorb it.” The only solution, he said, is “to raise the bar on quality,” adding, “I’m very excited about where that high quality is going to lead.”

	But won’t AI replace the humans doing work beneath the highest creative levels? The people making the stage backdrops for the Mozarts? Not necessarily, said Hughes: “If you want to produce something for the ages, you need many humans involved in that loop.”

	There is also the concern that AI strip-mines content without compensating its creators. But at AGBO, Brearton said, “We track every single tool and every single usage of every single tool. We’re very comprehensive about copyright and the paper trail of who did what … You have to be intentional about this. This is not ‘let’s do something on the fly.’”
	

	The future of entertainment, Brearton said, is “concurrence.” He used the example of his son, who consumes several different media at once on his various devices. “There are four or five different sources coming into him,” he said. “That’s different from the way I would consume entertainment, but that’s the future.”

	Those supplying that entertainment, he added, must have “the ability to build worlds that tell stories across all of those platforms concurrently and provide quality entertainment to that fan across those screens at the same time in a genuine way.”

	“And underlying all that, you still have to create incredible stories with wonderful characters in a rich world to live in,” he said.

	The keynote was moderated by Variety‘s Asia Editor Naman Ramachandran.

schema.headline: AI Can Critique Shakespeare but Can’t Write It, Russo Brothers’ AGBO Execs Tell Tokyo Market

title: Busan Winner ‘Birds in the Dark’ to Close Dharamshala International Film Festival, Varun Grover’s ‘Damned’ Among New Titles
description: Shashank Walia’s “Birds in the Dark,” about a call center executive whom a police informer mistakes for a suspect, will close the 15th Dharamshala
body:
Shashank Walia’s “Birds in the Dark,” about a call center executive whom a police informer mistakes for a suspect, will close the 15th Dharamshala International Film Festival with its India premiere. The festival runs Oct. 29–Nov. 1 at Tibetan Children’s Village in Upper Dharamshala.

	Walia’s debut feature took two prizes at the Busan International Film Festival earlier this month.


	The latest additions to the lineup include “A Fox Under a Pink Moon” by Mehrdad Oskouei. He made the film with Afghan artist Soraya Akhlaghi, and it tracks her attempts to get to her mother in Austria. Paromita Vohra’s “Working Girls” looks at work done by women across India that often goes unseen.
	

	Yashasvi Juyal’s “The Ink Stained Hand and The Missing Thumb,” a South Asia premiere, unfolds at a lonely highway toll booth in northern India, where grief and memory disturb daily routine. Ridham Janve’s “Hunter’s Moon” takes place in the Upper Dhauladhar range.

	The shorts section includes the world premiere of Aastha Tiku’s “Dreamboat,” along with Arun Fulara’s “Hudke ki Pyaang Pyaang” and Varun Grover’s “Damned.”

	“Curation has always been at the heart of DIFF. While curating, we look for distinctive voices, boundary-pushing filmmaking and films that open up new ways of seeing and thinking. Over the years, this careful and considered approach has allowed DIFF to build a program that is diverse in geography, form and subject, while remaining true to its commitment to independent cinema,” said Bina Paul, the festival’s director of programming.
	

	As previously announced, Rima Das’ “Not a Hero” opens the festival with its South Asia premiere. Titles also include Óliver Laxe’s “Sirāt,” Shaunak Sen’s “Termite,” Gurvinder Singh’s “Rehmat,” Sara Dosa’s “Time and Water,” Dennis Harvey and Lars Lovén’s “Celtic Utopia” and Tanushree Das and Saumyananda Sahi’s “Shadowbox.” “Termite” will have its Asia premiere at the festival and “Rehmat” its India premiere.

	Away from the screenings, DIFF’s Himalayan Film Fellows initiative, backed this year by Arthshila, is working with seven filmmakers from the Indian Himalayan Region on their first or second fiction features. Their mentors are Dechen Roder, Umesh Kulkarni and Dominic Sangma. The festival, working with Royal Enfield Social Mission, is also completing 24 community screenings around Kangra this year, at venues that have included schools, nunneries and the district jail.

	Filmmakers Ritu Sarin and Tenzing Sonam launched DIFF in 2012.

	“When we started DIFF, we wanted to create a space in Dharamshala where independent films could be experienced in a communal setting, and where filmmakers and audiences could spend time with each other beyond the screening room. Fifteen years later, that spirit remains at the heart of the festival. We are excited to welcome everyone back to the mountains for this year’s landmark edition,” said Sarin and Sonam.

	The festival runs Oct. 29–Nov. 1 at Tibetan Children’s Village in Upper Dharamshala.

schema.headline: Busan Winner ‘Birds in the Dark’ to Close Dharamshala International Film Festival, Varun Grover’s ‘Damned’ Among New Titles

title: Jimmy Fallon and Jamie Lee Curtis Transform Into Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes to Spoof ‘You Can See Everything’
description: On Wednesday night’s episode of “The Tonight Show,” host Jimmy Fallon gave his best Nathan Fielder impression while guest Jamie Lee Curtis played E
body:
On Wednesday night’s episode of “The Tonight Show,” host Jimmy Fallon gave his best Nathan Fielder impression while guest Jamie Lee Curtis played Elizabeth Holmes to spoof A24’s buzzy documentary, “You Can See Everything.”

	“Now, be honest. Do you really want to be on the show tonight?” asks Fallon, doing his best Fielder impression. “Of course I do. I love talking to you,” responded Curtis with her best Holmes-like voice while donning a blonde wig and looking deeply into the late-night host’s eyes. “So, you’re not just here to promote your new show. ‘Newlyweds’?” “No, I’m engaging with you as a human being,” said Curtis. “Why would I deceive you? There’s no reason for me to do that. There’s nothing for me to deceive you on.”
	

	“Good chat,” concluded Fallon, but not before one last question: “You’re being real right now?” “I’m always being real,” responded Curtis. As Fallon leaves, she yells, “Thank God! Fuck, what an asshole!”

	As mentioned in the cold open, Curtis was on the show to promote “Newlyweds,” her new NBC sitcom that premiered on Oct. 23. The logline for the show, starring Téa Leoni and Tim Daly, describes it as “a later-in-life love story about a free-spirited woman and a buttoned-up professor who marry impetuously after a whirlwind courtship.”

	Curtis will appear on the show in a recurring guest star role, and also co-created it with Gail Lerner, who was fired from the show earlier this month for “creative differences.” In Lerner’s statement when the news broke, she described the experience working on the show as “the most joyous TV experience of my life.”
	

	“You Can See Everything,” which debuted in theaters earlier this month on Oct. 16, has been a hit both critically and at the box office, where it’s already grossed $45.1 million domestically to date. Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim quietly worked on the movie for more than three years, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

	Watch the full cold open here.

schema.headline: Jimmy Fallon and Jamie Lee Curtis Transform Into Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes to Spoof ‘You Can See Everything’

title: James Gunn Calls Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman the DCU’s ‘Diamond Characters,’ Says Krypto, John Stewart and Peacemaker Could ‘Turn Into Diamonds’
description: James Gunn has once again taken to Threads in defense of his DC universe, and this time, is clarifying his previously proposed eight- to 10-year ro
body:
James Gunn has once again taken to Threads in defense of his DC universe, and this time, is clarifying his previously proposed eight- to 10-year roadmap for the fictional world and making it clearer where each character stands within it. 

	“You can look at my quotes from January ’23 when we started and I said we were going to do exactly what we’re doing,” the DC Studios co-head wrote responding to a now-deleted post. “I said some stories would be standalone like the Guardians movies were (which is what Clayface is) and some stories would have part of a larger narrative structure, which is what the Superman Saga is. All that said, each piece of the larger story should work on its own with or without having to see everything else.”
	

	He continued in a second post: “ALSO, some things get conflated here. The often cited ‘8 to 10 year roadmap’ originally pitched wasn’t only story points (although that was a part of it), but also the plan for DC as a whole, including focusing on diamond characters (Superman, Batman, WW) as well as smaller characters we could turn into diamonds (Krypto, John Stewart, Peacemaker), how we would foster filmmaker freedom & allow for multiple tones & ratings, the influences of Star Wars & George RR Martin, and so much more.”

	Gunn’s note about the “8 to 10 year roadmap” refers to his and fellow co-head Peter Safran’s 2022 remarks during a virtual Warner Bros. Discovery town hall, during which he’d said they’d mapped out an 8- to ten-year plan for DC. In a third post, he added: “It’s exciting seeing things START to come together and all that makes me even more excited for what we have in store for everyone in Man of Tomorrow.”
	

	On Saturday, Gunn took to the social media platform to defend his decision to expand the DC universe with “individual stories” amid criticism that his films aren’t building toward a major crossover event.

	Responding to a commenter who pointed out that Gunn doesn’t necessarily need to lay the foundation for one totally interconnected universe, he wrote, “I couldn’t agree more.” “DCU is just an alternate universe; we can enter at any location or time and tell THAT story. I dislike the idea that individual stories aren’t meaningful unless they lead to something else. People not understanding this is strange to me, because ‘Star Wars’ has essentially been doing this for 50 years across movies, shows, games and books, admittedly without the tonal variety,” he wrote.

	Gunn’s next film, “Superman: Man of Tomorrow,” hits theaters July 9, 2027.

schema.headline: James Gunn Calls Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman the DCU’s ‘Diamond Characters,’ Says Krypto, John Stewart and Peacemaker Could ‘Turn Into Diamonds’

title: Japan IP Market to Return to Cannes in 2027 as Tokyo Partnership Continues
description: The Japan IP Market will be back in Cannes next May for a second straight year. The Cannes Film Market and TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo
body:
The Japan IP Market will be back in Cannes next May for a second straight year. The Cannes Film Market and TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival, are again teaming up on the event, and the 2027 edition will run May 14-15.

	The return was revealed at TIFFCOM in Tokyo, during a conference on how Japan can forge new international partnerships after its stint as Country of Honor in Cannes. Alexandra Zakharchenko, head of industry programs at the Cannes Film Market, was among the panelists.
	

	“The success of Japan, Country of Honor showed what can happen when a focused national presence creates lasting opportunities for the industry. The Japan IP Market is one of those outcomes: a collaboration that extends beyond a single edition and gives Japanese intellectual properties greater access to international partners,” said Guillaume Esmiol, executive director of the Cannes Film Market. “I’m delighted that we are continuing this work with TIFFCOM to create more opportunities for rights holders to connect with international producers and partners, develop new adaptations and bring their stories to global audiences.”

	The Japan IP Market first ran in May 2026, one of the initiatives tied to Japan’s turn as Country of Honor at the Cannes Film Market. It put Japanese rights holders in the same room as industry professionals from abroad via pitches, one-on-one meetings and industry discussions. Kadokawa, Shochiku and Toei Company were among the companies taking part. The speaker lineup included Fujimura Tetsu, executive producer of “One Piece” and founder and CEO of Filosophia, Inc.
	

	“The Japan IP Market is about creating the right conditions for business opportunities between Japanese rights holders and international companies,” said Zakharchenko. “By bringing them together in Cannes, we can help turn growing interest in Japanese content into concrete adaptation deals and acquisitions, while fostering new collaboration opportunities.”

	Shiina Yasushi, executive adviser at UNIJAPAN and CEO of TIFFCOM, said the partnership with the Cannes market plays an important role for Japan’s audiovisual industry. He described the Cannes market as the biggest market attached to any film festival in the world. “Meeting the international professionals who gather there and creating together with them is the key to nurturing Japanese IP into global content,” he said.

	Ikeda Kaori, managing director of TIFFCOM, said the first edition had shown how keen producers and partners worldwide are on Japanese IP. “Through the continued partnership linking Cannes in May with the Tokyo IP Market in October, we are pleased to offer more professionals the opportunity to meet Japanese rights holders directly and discover the rich diversity of Japanese IP,” she said.

	The 2027 roster of companies and the rest of the program will be unveiled in the months ahead.

schema.headline: Japan IP Market to Return to Cannes in 2027 as Tokyo Partnership Continues

title: Celebrity Dog Broker Allegedly Ran Puppy Laundering Scheme Selling Breeder Dogs As Rescues
description:
Dog Broker To The Stars
                          Ran 'Puppy Laundering' Scheme
body:
Dog Broker To The Stars
                          Ran 'Puppy Laundering' Scheme
                          ... Officials Claim
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The California dog rescue operation where Ellen DeGeneres, Jennifer Aniston, Chrissy Teigen, Kris Jenner and other Hollywood stars got their furry friends ran a puppy laundering scheme where they sold dogs from puppy mills under the guise that they were rescues ... at least according to city officials.
      
    
            According to a new legal complaint, obtained by TMZ, Wagmor and its founder Melissa Bacelar are being dragged to court over allegations that the dog rescue bought hundreds of pooches from commercial breeders and sold them in California as rescues who needed to be adopted.
      
    
            In the civil enforcement action, the Los Angeles City Attorney's Office alleges Wagmor's customers shelled out $650 to $1,500 in "adoption fees" for the pups ... but instead of actually rescuing dogs in need, the unsuspecting customers were directly financing Wagmor's commercial breeding operation. The officials are looking to block the business from operating in this way and hit Wagmor with millions of dollars in civil penalties over the alleged practices.
      
    
            What's more, the City Attorney claims Bacelar used deception to solicit public donations ... they say she manufactured urgency and would tell people "breeders will kill dogs, including by shooting them" unless Wagmor raised sufficient funds fast.
      
    
            According to the docs, Wagmor bought the dogs from breeders all over the country ... and told donors their contributions were tax-deductible even after the IRS and California Franchise Tax Board revoked their tax-exempt status.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            It appears Jennifer, Ellen, Chrissy and Kris seemingly thought they were getting rescues from Wagmor ... they made social media posts showing off their dogs and announced they were adopting "rescued" pooches.
      
    
            Wagmor's founder, Melissa Bacelar, tells TMZ ... "The allegations against me are not true. Not some of them. Not most of them. They are not true, and I will prove it."
